# 🚨 CVE-2026-46242 - `BadEpoll`
**CVE-2026-46242** is a **Use-After-Free (UAF)** vulnerability in the Linux Kernel's **eventpoll (`epoll`)** implementation.

Bad Epoll (CVE-2026-46242) is a race-condition use-after-free in the Linux kernel's
`epoll` subsystem. This bug lets an unprivileged process become root, not only on Linux desktops and servers but also on Android devices.

More details are available in the full exploit [writeup](https://github.com/J-jaeyoung/security-research/blob/submit-cve-2026-46242/pocs/linux/kernelctf/CVE-2026-46242_lts_cos/docs/exploit.md) and [code](https://github.com/J-jaeyoung/security-research/blob/submit-cve-2026-46242/pocs/linux/kernelctf/CVE-2026-46242_lts_cos/exploit/lts-6.12.67/exploit.cpp).

Date: 2026-07-03 23:42:00 Author: HKLUG Team Title: CVE-2026-46242: 'Bad Epoll' Use-After-Free Flaw Grants Local Root Across Linux and Android Content:

A critical use-after-free race condition in the Linux kernel, tracked as CVE-2026-46242 and dubbed “Bad Epoll,” enables unprivileged local users to escalate privileges to root. The vulnerability affects Linux desktops, enterprise servers, and Android devices, with an upstream patch now available. While the core fix has been merged, the disclosure serves as an immediate technical advisory for administrators managing heterogeneous fleets and underscores the ongoing complexity of securing foundational kernel subsystems.

The flaw originates in the epoll subsystem, which manages I/O event notifications across multiple file descriptors. A race condition in the subsystem’s memory handling allows a local attacker to trigger a use-after-free scenario, bypassing standard privilege boundaries to execute arbitrary code with root permissions. Because exploitation requires only local access, the vulnerability presents a severe risk to shared computing environments, cloud infrastructure, and multi-tenant architectures where strict process isolation is critical.

The vulnerable code resides in the same kernel region where Anthropic’s AI model, Mythos, recently identified a separate bug. While the model successfully flagged that adjacent issue, it did not detect CVE-2026-46242. This gap highlights a broader industry reality: machine learning-driven security tools excel at pattern recognition and known vulnerability classes but frequently struggle with complex, low-level kernel state-management logic. Security teams should treat AI-assisted auditing as a supplementary validation layer, not a replacement for established fuzzing, static analysis, and human-led code review.

# Analysis Reasoning for CVE-2026-46242.yml

## bug_class
The commit message and code diff describe a classic use-after-free (UAF) scenario. The problem is that ep_remove() clears file->f_ep under file->f_lock, but continues to use the file pointer after this, while a concurrent __fput() can free the struct file and the associated struct eventpoll. This leads to hlist_del_rcu() writing into freed memory, specifically into the kmalloc-192 slab where the eventpoll was just freed. The patch fixes this by pinning the file object via epi_fget(), ensuring its refcount cannot reach zero and thus preventing __fput() from freeing the object while it is still in use. The commit message explicitly describes two UAFs: one on struct file and one on struct eventpoll, both due to lifetime mismanagement and race conditions. The code change adds a reference count increment (pin) and checks for successful pinning before proceeding, which is a standard fix for UAF. There are no new NULL pointer dereference checks or bounds checks; the root cause is accessing memory after it has been freed, not dereferencing a NULL pointer. Therefore, the bug class is UAF.

## impact
The vulnerability is a use-after-free (UAF) in the Linux kernel's eventpoll subsystem, specifically in ep_remove and related functions. The commit message describes a scenario where struct file and struct eventpoll can be freed while still being accessed, due to improper synchronization and reference counting. This UAF is reachable via epoll, a common syscall interface used by unprivileged userspace processes to monitor file descriptors. Attackers can exploit this by triggering epoll watches on other epoll instances, causing the kernel to access freed memory. Since struct file is SLAB_TYPESAFE_BY_RCU and can be recycled, attackers can heap spray to reclaim the freed object, potentially gaining control over kernel data structures. This is a classic kernel UAF scenario, which is well-known to be exploitable for local privilege escalation (LPE) by unprivileged users. The vulnerability is not restricted to privileged contexts, and the affected code is part of a widely used syscall interface. Therefore, the impact is LPE.

The epoll subsystem (`fs/eventpoll.c`) is the Linux kernel's high-performance I/O event notification facility, used extensively by virtually all server software (nginx, Apache, Node.js), desktop applications, web browsers (including Chrome), and Android system services. It cannot be disabled or compiled out -- any system running a vulnerable kernel version is exposed. The subsystem is approximately 2,500 lines of code, and a single commit in April 2023 introduced two separate race conditions into it, both of which turned out to be critical privilege escalation bugs (CVE-2026-43074 and CVE-2026-46242).

# Technical Analysis Report: Linux "Bad Epoll" CVE-2026-46242 (2026-07-07)

Prepared by: Actioner

CVE-2026-46242, dubbed "Bad Epoll," is a critical use-after-free vulnerability in the Linux kernel's epoll subsystem (`fs/eventpoll.c`) that allows any unprivileged local user to escalate privileges to root. The flaw is a race condition in the file-release path: when one eventpoll file descriptor monitors another and both are closed simultaneously, `ep_remove()` clears `file->f_ep` under `file->f_lock` while continuing to use the `@file` pointer, enabling a concurrent `__fput()` to free the object prematurely. The resulting 8-byte use-after-free write is converted into full kernel memory control via a cross-cache attack, arbitrary kernel read through `/proc/self/fdinfo`, and a ROP chain for root shell execution.
